title: The Great Amen and the Our Father
hookLine: the whole church says one loud Amen, then his own prayer
carry: so be it, all of us

cards: In the generations after the apostles, a Christian teacher in Rome named Justin wrote a defense of the faith addressed to the emperor.
People were spreading rumors about what Christians did at their secret gatherings, and he wanted to set the record straight. So he described a Sunday. They meet, he wrote.
They read from the apostles and the prophets. Someone preaches. They pray.
Bread and wine and water are brought. The one presiding gives thanks at length. And then all the people present answer with one word.

teach.b: The word is Amen, from a Hebrew root meaning firm, solid, reliable.

teach.h: THROUGH HIM, WITH HIM, IN HIM.
teach.b: At Mass, the long prayer over the bread and wine ends with the priest lifting both high, the bread and the cup together, and singing that through Christ, with him and in him, all glory and honor belong to the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit.

In Latin, Per ipsum, et cum ipso, et in ipso. And the whole church answers: Amen. It's called the Great Amen, often sung, sometimes repeated: the people's signature on everything the priest has just prayed.
Saint Jerome wrote that in Rome the Amen boomed out like thunder from heaven. Then, straight after, everyone stands and prays the Our Father together.
In the Douay-Rheims it opens: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name."
It's the prayer Jesus taught his friends, and it's here for a reason. It asks for daily bread, just before the bread is shared. It asks to forgive, just before the sign of peace.
At Mass, one thing is different. After deliver us from evil, the priest keeps going with a short prayer for peace and freedom from anxiety.
Then everyone ends together, giving God the kingdom, the power and the glory, now and forever. Some churches say that line straight after the prayer; at Mass, it comes here.

teach.h: OUR FATHER WHO ART IN HEAVEN, HALLOWED BE THY NAME.
teach.b: First a whole church signs its name. Then it prays like a family.

how: At the end of the Eucharistic Prayer the priest raises the consecrated bread and chalice and the congregation responds with the Great Amen, often sung; then all stand to pray the Lord's Prayer, followed by the priest's prayer for peace and the people's closing doxology.

practice: Think of something you agree with deep down: a hope for someone, a thing you know is true, something good you want to happen.
If you pray, say amen to it, out loud if you can, like a signature, not a murmur; if you don't, say yes to it instead, firmly. Notice the difference between agreeing and signing.
